headline: Connecticut energy strategy comment deadline puts rate design and reliability questions before the public
dek: DEEP is accepting written input until 4 p.m. Friday on 12 questions that will shape the scope of the state’s 2026-27 energy strategy, including affordability, electrification, infrastructure and climate resilience.
body: Connecticut residents, businesses and energy-sector organizations have until 4 p.m. Eastern on Friday to weigh in on the state’s next Comprehensive Energy Strategy, a planning process that could influence utility programs, legislation and future infrastructure decisions. The [Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection’s September 17 notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/deep-seeks-broad-public-input-on-development-of-connecticuts-next-comprehensive-energy-strategy) says written comments are being requested on the questions the agency should examine as it develops the 2026-27 strategy.

The deadline is for early input on the scope of the strategy, not a vote on a finished plan or an immediate change to electric, gas or transportation-fuel prices. DEEP said it began developing the document in July and will use the comment period to identify the issues, evidence and policy choices that deserve attention before recommendations are written. The agency also said additional opportunities for public participation will come later in the process.

The request covers more than the electric grid. DEEP said the strategy will assess electricity, natural gas, delivered fuels such as heating oil and propane, and transportation fuels including gasoline and diesel. It will also draw on Connecticut’s Integrated Resources Plan, a separate planning process that examines future electricity demand and the mix of conservation, generation and transmission resources that could meet it.

A [September 22 legal alert from Harris Beach Murtha](https://www.harrisbeachmurtha.com/insights/deep-seeks-input-on-key-issues-shaping-connecticuts-energy-future/) described the request as 12 strategic questions organized around three broad areas. The first is affordability, customers and communities: how to address energy burden, customer protections, electric and gas rate design, environmental justice and the distribution of costs and clean-energy benefits.

The second area is how Connecticut builds and manages its energy system. The questions include future demand, the siting and interconnection of new resources, coordination across fuel sectors, permitting, infrastructure investment, resource procurement, and workforce and supply-chain constraints. The notice also points to data-center growth as one factor that could affect planning for new electricity demand, although it does not make a final forecast for that demand.

The third area is climate, markets and resilience. DEEP is asking how Connecticut can pursue its climate goals while protecting affordability and reliability, how energy-related benefits should be measured, and how federal policy, ISO New England markets, fuel markets, supply chains and extreme weather should be considered. Those questions matter to ratepayers because choices about new equipment, generation and grid upgrades can distribute costs differently among households, businesses and customer classes.

The strategy is being prepared under Connecticut’s statutory energy-planning framework and in consultation with state agencies and entities including the departments of Agriculture, Economic and Community Development, Housing and Transportation, the Office of Policy and Management, the Office of Consumer Counsel, the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority and the Connecticut Green Bank. DEEP’s energy-policy office says the broader goal is an energy future that is clean, economical, resilient and reliable, while its public materials identify affordability and dependable service as parallel concerns.

For the public, the practical significance is that the state is still deciding which tradeoffs to study before it proposes a direction. Comments can describe household energy burdens, business and municipal needs, reliability concerns, infrastructure experience or data that should inform the work. DEEP directs people to its public notice and Energy Web Filing System for participation. After today’s deadline, the agency is expected to continue stakeholder engagement before issuing the strategy; the eventual document, rather than this comment period, will determine what recommendations move forward.
